column2: Samuel ministers to the Lord before Eli; the word is precious and no distinct vision occurs in those days.
column3: Precious for timion can imply rarity in context; distinct for diastellousa is provisional and does not claim a complete theory of revelation.

column2: Eli sleeps in his place with eyes growing heavy and inability to see, continuing into the nighttime setting of verse 3.
The lamp is not yet put in order, while Samuel sleeps in the sanctuary with the ark; the selected preparation verb is not changed to extinguishing.
column3: The precise lamp-maintenance action of episkeuazo remains a lexical question; no new timing inference is added beyond before.

column2: The Lord calls Samuel twice by name and receives Here I am; the doubled name and presentative response remain.
Samuel runs to Eli, repeats Here I am and attributes the call to him; Eli denies calling and commands return and sleep, which Samuel does.
The Lord again doubles Samuel's name; Samuel's second visit repeats the mistaken attribution and Eli's denial and sleep instruction.
The explanatory aside places this before Samuel's knowledge of God and revelation of the Lord's word to him; both clauses remain.
The third call brings another visit and repeated response, after which Eli realizes the Lord is calling; the sequence is not shortened.
Eli's ordinary you instructions contain a nested direct prayer with Thy servant hears; the address rule follows the actual speaker and addressee.
The Lord comes and stands, calls as before, and Samuel answers Speak, for Thy servant hears; Lord from verse 9 is not inserted into the shorter response.
Behold introduces the Lord's carrying out His words in Israel so that every hearer's two ears resound; both ears and the sound image remain.
Everything spoken concerning Eli's house will be raised against him, beginning and completion both explicit.
The Lord announces continuing vengeance for the sons' wrongs: they revile God, and Eli fails to admonish them even so.
column3: God is the selected object of reviling, not a substituted themselves; the final even-so phrase remains.

column2: The oath rules out expiation of Eli's house's wrongdoing by incense or sacrifices for ever.
column3: Never represents the negative force of the ei oath formula with the continuing-time phrase; it is not a simple conditional if translated as a new proposition.

column2: Samuel lies until morning, rises early and opens the Lord's doors, while fearing to report the vision; both morning references remain.
Eli calls Samuel child and receives another Here I am; the familiar response remains consistent through the calling account.
The request for the spoken word becomes an oath against concealing any of all the words heard; repeated these things and the ears image remain.
Samuel reports every word and conceals nothing; Eli identifies the Lord and states that He will do what is good before Him, retaining the future rather than a wish.
Samuel grows with the Lord present, and none of his words falls to the ground; the fulfilled-word image remains.
column3: The possessive his may refer contextually to Samuel's prophetic words or to the Lord's words; inherited lower-case spelling does not resolve the Greek antecedent.

column2: All Israel from Dan to Beersheba recognizes Samuel as faithful in prophetic service to the Lord; both geographic limits remain.
The Lord continues self-disclosure at Shiloh, Samuel's prophetic recognition extends end to end, and the longer ending reports Eli's age and his sons' evil way.
column3: The repeated going construction is rendered continued on their way; no shorter chapter ending replaces the full selected unit.

column2: The foreigners gather and Israel meets them, with camps at Ebenezer and Aphek; the selected military opening is retained.
The battle turns, Israel stumbles and four thousand are struck in the field formation; the selected count and defeat image remain.
The elders attribute the stumble to the Lord and propose bringing the ark from Shiloh to save them; the ark's saving action remains their expressed expectation.
The ark of the Lord seated upon cherubim is brought from Shiloh with Hophni and Phinehas; the divine throne description and both sons remain.
The ark's arrival triggers all Israel's loud cry and the earth's resounding, preserving the audible narrative link to the foreigners' response.
Foreigners is repeated as the hearers and speakers who inquire about the Hebrews' great cry, then learn of the ark's arrival.
Fear leads to a plural-gods statement, woe, direct Rescue us today, Lord, and the claim of unprecedented events; the surprising direct appeal remains.
column3: Before renders yesterday and the third day as the familiar prior-time idiom; no singular god replaces the quoted plural.

column2: The second woe and rescue question concern these powerful gods who struck Egypt with every plague and in the wilderness; the difficult final location remains.
Two be-men exhortations surround the warning against serving Hebrews as they served us, followed by the fight command; repetition is retained.
Israel stumbles and each flees home, with very great slaughter and thirty thousand troops fallen; troops represents the military-unit term in context.
The ark is captured and both sons die, explicitly named Hophni and Phinehas; the event answers the earlier sign without added explanation.
A Benjaminite runs from battle to Shiloh the same day with torn clothes and earth on his head; the mourning signs remain.
Behold introduces seated Eli watching the road with a distraught heart over the ark; the messenger enters and the city cries out.
column3: Watching the road is retained beside the following blindness notice without harmonizing the apparent tension.

column2: Eli hears and questions the cry, and the messenger hurries in to report; the repeated sound language remains.
The selected age is ninety, with fixed eyes and no sight; Eli asks the men around him about the uproar.
column3: Fixed for epanestesan is an inherited eye-description interpretation requiring lexical review; the number is not changed to ninety-eight.

column2: Propose Eli said before What happened, child to distinguish the questioner from the returning messenger in natural spoken English.
column3: The Greek question's subject is unexpressed; Eli is inferred from the dialogue and child-address, not a newly explicit Greek name in that clause.

column2: The young messenger reports Israel's flight, great slaughter, both sons' deaths and the ark's capture in that order; the losses are not collapsed.
Mention of the ark precedes Eli's backward fall, crushed back and death because of age and weight; twenty years of judging remains.
column3: The inherited explicit messenger/Eli names clarify two unexpressed Greek subjects. Back is not changed to neck, nor twenty to forty.

column2: Phinehas's pregnant wife hears of ark, father-in-law and husband, then crouches and gives birth as pains turn upon her; all three losses remain.
The dying woman hears the attendants' reassurance that she bore a son but neither answers nor understands in her heart.
column3: Was dying gives the historical present death verb an unfolding sense in the birth scene; the exact narrative timing is not independently resolved.

column2: Woe-barchaboth preserves the selected naming expression and its association with ark, father-in-law and husband; no familiar Ichabod substitution is made.
column3: The relation of the lament Woe to the name barchaboth requires naming/apparatus review; the inherited combined form remains provisional.

column2: They say that Israel's glory has been carried away with the Lord's ark's capture; the final plural speaker is not changed to she.
